title: How I use LLMs to learn complex topics
titleZh: 我如何利用法学硕士学习复杂的主题
author: laurentiurad
relevanceReason: 命中 2 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: Many engineers I know use generative AI for many functions, like building PoCs, internal tools or dashboards, or even learning new stuff. I personally find the style used by LLMs to explain things difficult to follow. It's just too simplistic and depending on the number of emojis used, a bit annoying too.

While I was analyzing new AI bottlenecks that might slow down data center buildup, I realized there are many aspects of chip production that I do not know. Surfing the web, I asked myself what if there would be a game to get you through the process of building a chip at a fab? For sure learning this way will stick, since you can map concepts with objects within the game. This is when I decided to try it, and it actually turned out really well. The flow Instead of just asking AI to explain a topic, I use the following flow:

In plan mode (using CC, or OpenCode) I ask a model to build the foundational knowledge for X topic. I ask it to review the accuracy of the knowledge base it built in the previous step. I proceed asking it to build a simulation of that topic in a low-poly, Rollercoaster Tycoon-like animation. I add some UX elements as well, like the page needs to be visible on both large and small screens, have controls to stop the flow whenever I want etc. I then push it to a new repo and enable GitHub Pages for it.

The result What you get is a beautiful animation that is 100% accurate and free of hallucinations. For me, this method works a lot better than just reading endless materials that I find on Google, or trying to digest a bulleted list that is spat by a language model. I've done this specifically for learning chip building and launch it under this website: ChipTycoon. You get to follow a cart from the moment when sand is collected, to the moment when a chip is finalized and delivered to a data center. Visually, you can follow the cart and see how it changes too. Since it's low-poly, the details might be missing, but it's still a good indicator for showing how the product changes once it goes through the many steps required in the manufacturing process. How to improve it further Let's say that the low-poly design requires to much immagination to actually visualize what happened to the quartz sand pile after it left the furnace. To transform this into a more realistic representation, you can use my skill for transforming pictures into 3d objects, and map the resulting objects to your simulation. This way you get more accurate design. Also, you can add challenges to your simulation too. Trying to answer questions about a previous step in the chip manufacturing process will help you retain the knowledge tremendously. Add intuitive puzzles too that will help you learn even better. Check out what other pages I created:
How rocket engines are made How LLMs work How F1 engines are built How an EUV machine is built

comments.author: matherial
comments.textRawHtml:
This is, without exaggeration, probably the fiftieth blog post or long-form comment about how someone is using an LLM for "complex learning", and I'd just really like to see at least one of these to be accompanied by a statement saying what are the kinds of problems the author can now confidently solve that they couldn't before.

In my experience, LLMs are really good for taking up your time and making you feel like you're learning, in the same way that many of the popular educational videos on YouTube are fun to watch and don't really teach you anything.

If you ask an LLM to give you a 500-word summary of quantum physics, it'll give you an oversimplification that probably leans on a hodgepodge of pop-sci metaphors. And if you start drilling down, you risk drilling down on these ELI5 metaphors, which can get you farther away from truth.
comments.textZhHtml:
毫不夸张地说，这可能是第五十篇关于某人如何使用 LLM 进行“复杂学习”的博客文章或长篇评论，我真的很希望看到其中至少一篇附有一份声明，说明作者现在可以自信地解决哪些以前无法解决的问题。

根据我的经验，LLM 非常适合占用您的时间，让您感觉自己正在学习，就像 YouTube 上许多流行的教育视频看起来很有趣，但并没有真正教你任何东西一样。

如果你要求法学硕士给你一份 500 字的量子物理学摘要，它会给你一个过于简单化的结果，很可能依赖于流行科学隐喻的大杂烩。如果你开始深入研究，你就有可能深入了解这些 ELI5 隐喻，这会让你离真相越来越远。

children.author: manfromchina1
children.textRawHtml:
I personally don't get this attitude. For one thing, nobody on earth can give you a 500-word summary of quantum physics in a way that lets you internalize even a tiny bit of it. That's not how you learn anything.

Here's how I do it: I open Baby Rudin (3rd ed.), second chapter, and read the main text - absolute brutality. I unpack almost every sentence with Claude/GPT until I finally get what's going on. No ELI5 nonsense, just examples and counterexamples galore while absorbing the techniques and the way of thinking in analysis/topology. How do I know I've learned the material? By solving every single problem in that chapter. Here's the thing, though: the problems in Rudin can be brutal and decoupled from what's in the text, so if you can handle them, you've definitely mastered the material. No 500-word summary of analysis here.
children.textZhHtml:
我个人不理解这种态度。一方面，地球上没有人能为你提供 500 字的量子物理学摘要，让你内化哪怕是一小部分。这不是你学习任何东西的方式。

我是这样做的：我打开《Baby Rudin》（第三版）第二章，然后阅读正文 - 绝对的残酷。我用 Claude/GPT 解开几乎每句话，直到我最终明白发生了什么。没有 ELI5 废话，只有大量的例子和反例，同时吸收分析/拓扑中的技术和思维方式。我怎么知道我已经学会了这些材料？通过解决该章中的每个问题。但事情是这样的：Rudin 中的问题可能很残酷，并且与文本中的内容脱节，所以如果你能处理它们，你肯定已经掌握了这些材料。这里没有 500 字的分析摘要。

children.author: turzmo
children.textRawHtml:
Baby Rudin is a special textbook: it comes from a time when mathematics textbooks were not at all judged by their pedagogical value, but instead by their aesthetic appeal to mathematicians (a la Bourbaki).

If you actually want to learn analysis, there are a nearly infinite number of friendlier resources (e.g., Understanding Analysis by Abbott).

Learning to unpack difficult text on one’s own is a valuable skill. Research papers often require a similar amount of suffering, and at the frontier of knowledge, despite all the advances we’ve seen, LLMs seem to have absolutely no understanding or intuition. They are much better at things that have been expounded at length by humans before.

I would argue that if you’re going to use an LLM to make Rudin easier to understand, you are not learning how to absorb difficult material, nor are you learning analysis efficiently.
children.textZhHtml:
《Baby Rudin》是一本特殊的教科书：它来自一个时代，那时数学教科书根本不以教学价值为标准，而是以它们对数学家的审美吸引力（布尔巴基那样）来评判。

如果你真的想学习分析，这里有几乎无限数量的更友好的资源（例如 Abbott 的《理解分析》）。

学会自己解开困难的文本是一项宝贵的技能。研究论文通常需要类似的痛苦，而在知识的前沿，尽管我们已经看到了所有的进步，法学硕士似乎完全没有理解或直觉。他们在人类之前详细阐述过的事情上要好得多。

我认为，如果你打算使用法学硕士来让 Rudin 更容易理解，你就不是在学习如何吸收困难的材料，也不是在有效地学习分析。

我认为，如果他能够在没有法学硕士帮助的情况下自己解决问题，那么他就已经掌握了它。

children.textRawHtml: That may be, but my point stands. It is neither learning to absorb difficult material nor efficient.
children.textZhHtml: 可能是这样，但我的观点是正确的。学习既不是吸收困难的材料，也不是高效的。

children.author: BeetleB
children.textRawHtml:
The same could be said for someone taking a university course where Rudin is the textbook, and they rely on the professor/TA to help them understand the book.

This is needlessly nitpicky. The stark reality is that the majority of undergrad math majors do not achieve what this person has merely be reading Rudin (assuming he is actually solving most/all the problems).
children.textZhHtml:
对于以 Rudin 为教科书的大学课程的人来说也是如此，他们依靠教授/助教来帮助他们理解这本书。

这是不必要的挑剔。严峻的现实是，大多数数学专业的本科生并没有达到这个人仅仅阅读鲁丁（假设他实际上正在解决大多数/所有问题）的程度。

children.author: turzmo
children.textRawHtml:
I don't think so. There are many objections to methods of making learning "easier" and the invalidity of one does not imply the invalidity of all of them.

We've also seen the effects of LLMs on learning, at least when used instinctively by students. An entire generation of students seems to have atrophied their critical thinking skills this way. Talk to 21-year-olds today and you'll see what I mean.
children.textZhHtml:
我不这么认为。对于让学习变得“更容易”的方法有很多反对意见，其中一种方法的无效并不意味着所有方法都无效。

我们也看到了法学硕士对学习的影响，至少在学生本能地使用时是这样。整整一代学生的批判性思维能力似乎都以这种方式退化了。今天与 21 岁的人交谈，您就会明白我的意思。

children.author: sublinear
children.textRawHtml:
Is that meaningfully different from the study methods of the past? That doesn't require an LLM, and using one risks correctness in exchange for speed. You might not even get that speed if you're stuck in the weeds often enough.

A decade ago, a google search for study guides written by another professor would have been slightly slower. A decade before that, you'd be even slower fumbling through several books. Every single word could at least be trusted. You don't get that from an LLM.
children.textZhHtml:
这与过去的学习方法有什么不同吗？这不需要法学硕士，并且使用法学硕士会冒着以正确性换取速度的风险。如果你经常陷入困境，你甚至可能无法达到这个速度。

十年前，在谷歌上搜索另一位教授撰写的学习指南会稍微慢一些。十年前，你翻阅几本书的速度甚至会更慢。至少每一个字都是可信的。这是你无法从法学硕士那里得到的。

children.author: cornholio
children.textRawHtml:
> Is that meaningfully different from the study methods of the past?

The fundamental service a teacher provides is personalized feedback, quickly identifying where you are stuck and focusing the explanations and exercises on that area, drastically increasing the speed and quality of learning versus the self-supervised route.

The lack of this closed loop effectively killed the high hopes that were placed in e-learning and MOOCs 15-20 years ago, TV learning in the 1960s and many other failed revolutions, seems every generation has its own version.

It appears to me LLMs have a real potential to close this loop and become the failed educational revolution of our own generation.
children.textZhHtml:
> 这与过去的学习方法有本质上的不同吗？

教师提供的基本服务是个性化反馈，快速识别你的困境，并针对该领域进行重点讲解和练习，与自我监督的路线相比，大大提高了学习的速度和质量。

缺乏这种闭环，有效地扼杀了 15-20 年前对电子学习和 MOOC 的厚望，以及现在的电视学习。 20 世纪 60 年代和许多其他失败的革命，似乎每一代人都有自己的版本。

在我看来，法学硕士确实有潜力结束这个循环，成为我们这一代失败的教育革命。

children.author: alper
children.textRawHtml:
> personalized feedback, quickly identifying where you are stuck and focusing the explanations and exercises on that area,

This has been a huge blocker when I tried to study advanced math myself. Many of the exercise books don't have worked out answers, so often you're either stuck or you have to hunt a variety of sources online for solutions and advice. It kills flow.
children.textZhHtml:
> 个性化反馈，快速识别您陷入困境的地方，并将解释和练习集中在该领域，

当我尝试自己学习高等数学时，这一直是一个巨大的障碍。许多练习册都没有答案，因此您常常要么陷入困境，要么必须在网上寻找各种资源来寻求解决方案和建议。它会扼杀流量。

children.author: Jtarii
children.textRawHtml:
If you have an actual mathematics professor to ask questions to then sure do that, but most people don't have that luxury. Also the error rate of frontier LLMs on textbook highschool/college level mathematics is going to be extremely low.

It is also significantly more engaging and fun.
children.textZhHtml:
如果你有一位真正的数学教授来提问，那么你一定要这么做，但大多数人都没有这种奢侈。此外，前沿法学硕士在高中/大学水平数学课本上的错误率将极低。

它也明显更具吸引力和乐趣。
